claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Active CaMKII/UNC-43 functions cell-autonomously to suppress axon degeneration.
claims.source: These data indicate that active CaMKII/UNC-43 functions cell-autonomously to suppress axon degeneration.

claims.claim: WT UNC-43 cannot be adequately activated even when overexpressed in PVQ axons without mitochondria.

claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of WT vs CA UNC-43 overexpression.

claims.claim: In ric-7(n2657) animals CaMKII/UNC-43 abundance in distal axons is dramatically reduced (37% of the control levels).

claims.claim: CaMKII/UNC-43 abundance in cell bodies is not affected in ric-7(n2657) animals.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and E using NATF labeling.

claims.claim: Axonal mitochondria promote CaMKII/UNC-43 localization in axons.

claims.claim: In C. elegans nervous system, CaMKII/UNC-43 has been shown to regulate asymmetric neural development through the conserved Sarm1/TIR-1-ASK1/NSY-1-p38 MAPK pathway.

claims.claim: Active TIR-1 recruits and activates the NSY-1 MAPKKK to inhibit the expression of specific odorant receptors.

claims.claim: UNC-43, TIR-1, and NSY-1 colocalize at synaptic regions of AWC and physically interact with each other to form a signaling complex.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The UNC-43/TIR-1/NSY-1 complex functions to suppress axon degeneration in the absence of mitochondria.

claims.claim: During development, the UNC-43/TIR-1/NSY-1 complex regulates asymmetric neuronal development via the MAPKK SEK-1 and two redundant p38 MAPKs, PMK-1 and PMK-2.
claims.source: During development, this complex regulates asymmetric neuronal development via the MAPKK SEK-1 and two redundant p38 MAPKs, PMK-1 and PMK-2 (Alqadah et al., 2016b; Pagano et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Loss of the downstream C/EBP bZIP transcription factor CEBP-1 largely blocks the protective effects of activated CaMKII.
claims.source: By contrast, loss of another p38 MAPK, PMK-3, or loss of its downstream C/EBP bZIP transcription factor CEBP-1 (Yan et al., 2009) largely blocks the protective effects of activated CaMKII (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and a citation.

claims.claim: Active CaMKII protects against axon degeneration through CEBP-1-mediated transcription regulation.

claims.claim: Sarm1/TIR-1 is required for constitutively activated CaMKII to suppress degeneration due to mitochondria mislocalization.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: Sarm1/TIR-1 has a neuroprotective role as part of the UNC-43/TIR-1/NSY-1 signaling complex.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing TIR-1 is required for protection and overexpression suppresses degeneration.

claims.claim: The wp60 allele is a G-to-A point mutation at the splice acceptor site in the intron before the first KBS, and it affects all three casy-1 isoforms.

claims.claim: In the ric-7(n2657); casy-1(wp78) animals, PVQ axons rarely degenerate and only develop a few swellings during the L4-1doa transition.

claims.claim: The phenotype of ric-7(n2657); casy-1(wp78) is very similar to the protection conferred by activated CaMKII/UNC-43.

claims.claim: Expression of CASY-1 fragments #1–4, but not #5 or #6, caused strong PVQ degeneration in ric-7(n2657); casy-1(wp60) animals.
claims.source: Expression of CASY-1 fragments #1–4, but not #5 or #6, caused strong PVQ degeneration in ric-7(n2657); casy-1(wp60) animals (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Both calsyntenin's TM domain and the ICD are required for degeneration, while its extracellular region is dispensable.

claims.claim: Overexpressing CASY-1C in ric-7(n2657); casy-1(wp60) leads to near complete degeneration at L4, a timepoint at which only a few ric-7(n2657) control animals show degeneration.

claims.claim: Overexpressing CASY-1C in casy-1(wp60) single mutants does not induce degeneration.

results.result: PVQ axons lacking mitochondria undergo spontaneous age-dependent degeneration. Loss of ric-7, unc-116, or miro-1;mtx-2 results in complete absence of axonal mitochondria and completely penetrant axon degeneration in adults, with most degeneration occurring during the L4 to 1-day-old adult transition. Degeneration proceeds sequentially through swelling, thinning, fragmentation, and debris clearance. Mutants retaining some axonal mitochondria (miro-1;miro-2 or trak-1) do not show degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C43 provide converging evidence from multiple genetic backgrounds (ric-7, unc-116, miro-1;mtx-2) showing that complete loss of axonal mitochondria causes degeneration, while partial loss does not. The temporal progression is documented through longitudinal imaging (C43), and the causal relationship is confirmed by rescue experiments with the UNC-116::TOMM-7 chimera (C44-C45). The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

results.result: Constitutively active CaMKII/UNC-43 suppresses axon degeneration caused by loss of mitochondria without restoring mitochondrial localization. The wp64 allele (G207R mutation) and the canonical n498sd allele both confer strong protection (>80% intact axons at 5 days old adult), while loss-of-function unc-43(e408) does not suppress degeneration. This protection occurs across multiple genetic backgrounds lacking mitochondria (ric-7, unc-116, miro-1;mtx-2).
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C57 demonstrate through genetic analysis that constitutively active CaMKII suppresses degeneration in multiple independent genetic backgrounds. The molecular characterization of wp64 (C51) and phenotypic similarity to n498sd (C55-C56) support the constitutive activity interpretation. The lack of suppression by loss-of-function alleles (C57) and persistence of mitochondrial absence (C49) confirm the mechanism acts downstream of mitochondrial loss. Multiple independent alleles and genetic backgrounds provide strong support.

results.result: CaMKII/UNC-43 functions cell-autonomously to suppress degeneration, with constitutively active UNC-43 providing stronger protection (70% intact) than wildtype overexpression (20% intact). This suggests that wildtype UNC-43 cannot be adequately activated when overexpressed in axons lacking mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 demonstrate cell-autonomous function through PVQ-specific expression experiments. The differential effectiveness of CA versus WT overexpression (C64-C65) provides evidence for inadequate activation of WT protein in the absence of mitochondria (C67). However, the inference in C67 assumes that overexpression levels are comparable between WT and CA constructs, which is not directly demonstrated. The cell-autonomous conclusion (C66) is well-supported by the expression data.

results.result: Axonal mitochondria promote CaMKII/UNC-43 localization in axons. In ric-7(n2657) animals, CaMKII/UNC-43 abundance in distal axons is reduced to 37% of control levels, while cell body levels are unaffected. Forcing mitochondria into axons with the UNC-116::TOMM-7 chimera partially restores axonal CaMKII levels to 69% of control.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 use NATF labeling to quantify endogenous CaMKII levels in specific subcellular compartments. The selective reduction in axons but not cell bodies (C68-C69) and partial rescue by forced mitochondrial transport (C70) provide strong evidence for the conclusion (C71). The quantitative measurements and rescue experiment support a causal relationship between mitochondrial presence and CaMKII localization.

results.result: CaMKII/UNC-43 suppresses axon degeneration through the conserved Sarm1/TIR-1-ASK1/NSY-1-p38 MAPK pathway, specifically via PMK-3 and the transcription factor CEBP-1. Loss-of-function mutations in tir-1, nsy-1, pmk-3, or cebp-1 completely abolish protection by constitutively active unc-43, while loss of pmk-1 does not affect protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 demonstrate through genetic epistasis that the UNC-43/TIR-1/NSY-1 complex and downstream PMK-3/CEBP-1 are required for CaMKII-mediated protection. The specificity for PMK-3 over PMK-1 (C79-C80) is well-documented. The pathway is conserved (C72) and the genetic interactions are clear. The conclusion that this acts through transcriptional regulation (C82) is supported by the requirement for CEBP-1, though direct transcriptional targets are not identified.

results.result: Sarm1/TIR-1 has a neuroprotective role in this context, required for CaMKII-mediated suppression of degeneration. Loss-of-function tir-1 mutations do not suppress degeneration, NAD+ synthase overexpression does not suppress degeneration, but TIR-1 overexpression strongly suppresses degeneration. This contrasts with TIR-1's pro-degenerative role in Wallerian degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 establish a context-dependent neuroprotective role for TIR-1 through multiple lines of evidence: requirement for CaMKII-mediated protection (C83), lack of suppression by tir-1 loss-of-function (C85), lack of effect of NAD+ synthase overexpression (C86), and suppression by TIR-1 overexpression (C87). This is surprising given TIR-1's known pro-degenerative role in other contexts (C84), making the finding particularly significant. The evidence is internally consistent.

results.result: Loss of calsyntenin/CASY-1 prevents axon degeneration caused by lack of mitochondria. The wp60 allele (splice acceptor mutation) and wp78 deletion allele both strongly suppress degeneration in ric-7 and miro-1;mtx-2 mutants, with >80% of 5-day-old adults showing intact axons. Protection can be abolished by expressing a fosmid containing the endogenous casy-1 locus.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 demonstrate through multiple independent alleles (wp60, wp78) and genetic backgrounds (ric-7, miro-1;mtx-2) that loss of casy-1 suppresses degeneration. The molecular characterization of the alleles (C89) and rescue by the genomic locus (C93) confirm the genetic identity. The phenotypic similarity to CaMKII activation (C92) suggests a common pathway. The evidence is strong and well-controlled.

results.result: Calsyntenin's transmembrane domain and intracellular domain are required for its pro-degeneration function, while the extracellular region is dispensable. Structure-function analysis shows that CASY-1 fragments containing both TM and ICD (#1-4) restore degeneration, while fragments lacking either domain (#5-6) do not. The tm718 allele (extracellular deletion) does not suppress degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 use systematic structure-function analysis with six different fragments to map functional domains. The results are internally consistent: fragments with TM+ICD restore function, those lacking either do not. The tm718 allele provides independent confirmation that the extracellular domain is dispensable. The cell-autonomous rescue (C95) confirms the site of action. This is well-designed domain mapping.

results.result: Overexpressing CASY-1C enhances degeneration in the absence of mitochondria but does not induce degeneration in otherwise wild-type animals. In ric-7;casy-1(wp60) animals, CASY-1C overexpression causes near-complete degeneration at L4, while overexpression in casy-1(wp60) alone does not cause degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 demonstrate context-dependent effects of CASY-1 overexpression through comparison of different genetic backgrounds. The acceleration of degeneration in ric-7 background (C99) versus no effect in wild-type background (C100) supports the conclusion that CASY-1 enhances but does not initiate degeneration (C101). This suggests CASY-1 acts on a pathway activated by mitochondrial loss.

results.result: Calsyntenin's kinesin-binding sites are required for its pro-degeneration function, and a kinesin complex containing KLC-2 (but not KLC-1) regulates calsyntenin traffic to promote degeneration. Mutating the conserved tryptophans in the KBS to alanine eliminates pro-degeneration function, and klc-2 loss-of-function strongly suppresses degeneration while klc-1 loss does not.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 establish the requirement for kinesin binding through mutagenesis (C103) and genetic analysis (C104-C105). The specificity for KLC-2 over KLC-1 (C104-C105) is clearly demonstrated. The conclusion that KLC-2-containing kinesin regulates calsyntenin traffic (C106) is well-supported by the genetic and biochemical evidence, though direct trafficking measurements in klc-2 mutants are noted as not possible due to low signal.

results.result: CASY-1 localization in axons depends on KLC-2. Endogenous CASY-1 is visible throughout the axon in control animals, with no significant change in steady-state levels in ric-7 mutants. However, loss of KLC-2 causes dramatic redistribution to puncta in the cell body and proximal axon, with near-complete loss from distal axons and partial reduction in cell bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C112 use NATF labeling to track endogenous CASY-1 localization. The dramatic redistribution in klc-2 mutants (C109-C111) provides strong evidence for KLC-2-dependent axonal localization (C112). The lack of change in ric-7 mutants (C108) is interesting and suggests steady-state levels may not reflect trafficking dynamics. The quantitative measurements and clear phenotypic differences support the conclusions.

results.result: CASY-1C trafficking is highly anterogradely biased (81% anterograde) with speeds and run lengths consistent with kinesin-mediated transport. In ric-7 mutants, the anterograde bias is reduced (63%) and speeds/run lengths are dramatically reduced in both directions, suggesting trafficking depends on kinesin motors and is affected by loss of mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C117 provide live imaging data characterizing CASY-1 trafficking dynamics. The anterograde bias (C113) and quantitative parameters (C114-C115) are consistent with kinesin-mediated transport. The effects of ric-7 mutation (C116) are interesting but the interpretation is complicated by the use of overexpressed CASY-1C rather than endogenous protein. The conclusion about kinesin dependence (C117) is supported by the trafficking data and KLC-2 localization data, though direct demonstration in klc-2 mutants was not possible.

results.result: Mint/LIN-10 is a cargo of CASY-1 that is transported from cell body to distal axon to mediate degeneration. Two independent lin-10 loss-of-function alleles suppress degeneration, and in casy-1 mutants, LIN-10 abundance in distal axons is reduced to 56% of control while soma levels increase by 27%.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 establish LIN-10 as a CASY-1 cargo through genetic suppression (C124) and localization analysis (C125-C126). The reciprocal changes in axon versus soma (C125-C126) are consistent with a trafficking defect. The model (C127) is well-supported by the data, though direct demonstration of physical interaction or co-trafficking would strengthen the conclusion. The use of two independent lin-10 alleles (C124) strengthens the genetic evidence.

results.result: APP homolog APL-1 and the LIN-2/7/10 complex are not involved in spontaneous degeneration caused by loss of mitochondria. Cre-loxP knockout of apl-1 in PVQ and the apl-1(wp22) allele do not suppress degeneration, and lin-2 loss-of-function does not suppress degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C132 use multiple approaches (Cre-loxP knockout, existing alleles) to test involvement of APL-1 and the LIN-2/7/10 complex. The negative results are clearly documented and important for defining the pathway. The conclusion that these factors are not involved (C130, C132) is well-supported, though it's worth noting that negative results can be harder to interpret definitively. The use of multiple alleles and approaches strengthens confidence in the conclusions.

results.result: Loss of CASY-1, LIN-10, and KLC-2 act via the UNC-43-TIR-1-NSY-1-SEK-1-PMK-3-CEBP-1 pathway to protect against degeneration. Loss-of-function unc-43 largely abolishes protection in casy-1, lin-10, and klc-2 mutants, and loss of tir-1, nsy-1, sek-1, pmk-3, or cebp-1 all suppress casy-1 protection, while pmk-1/pmk-2 do not.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C139 establish through extensive genetic epistasis that the calsyntenin/Mint/KLC-2 complex acts upstream of the CaMKII-MAPK pathway. The requirement for unc-43 in all three suppressor backgrounds (C133-C134) and the systematic testing of downstream pathway components (C137-C138) provide strong evidence. The specificity for PMK-3 over PMK-1/PMK-2 (C138) is consistent with the CaMKII results. The cell-autonomous rescue (C136) confirms the site of action. This is thorough genetic pathway analysis.

results.result: CASY-1 and LIN-10 do not regulate CaMKII/UNC-43 protein levels in axons. Endogenous CaMKII levels in distal axons are not restored in ric-7;casy-1 or ric-7;lin-10 double mutants compared to ric-7 alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141 use NATF labeling to test whether casy-1 or lin-10 mutations affect CaMKII levels. The lack of restoration (C140) supports the conclusion that these factors do not regulate CaMKII abundance (C141). This is important for understanding the mechanism - the pathway likely acts through CaMKII activation rather than localization. The measurement is straightforward and the conclusion is well-supported.

results.result: The L-type voltage-gated calcium channel composed of EGL-19 and UNC-36 is required for axon protection in casy-1 and lin-10 mutants and acts upstream of CaMKII/UNC-43. Loss of egl-19 or unc-36 completely abolishes protection in casy-1 and lin-10 mutants, while loss of the non-L-type channel unc-2 has minimal effect. The channel is not required for protection by constitutively active CaMKII.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C147 establish through genetic epistasis that L-type VGCCs act upstream of CaMKII to mediate protection. The specificity for EGL-19/UNC-36 over UNC-2 (C144) and the bypass by constitutively active CaMKII (C146) clearly position the channel upstream of CaMKII activation (C147). The complete suppression of protection (C142-C143) demonstrates the requirement. This is well-designed epistasis analysis that establishes pathway order.

results.result: The VGCC-CaMKII/UNC-43 pathway is specifically required for axon protection in the context of mitochondria mislocalization, not for baseline axon stability. Loss of EGL-19, UNC-36, or CaMKII/UNC-43 does not trigger degeneration in wild-type animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C149 establish the context-dependence of the pathway through analysis of single mutants. The lack of degeneration in egl-19, unc-36, or unc-43 single mutants (C148) demonstrates that the pathway is not required for baseline axon maintenance, only for protection in the context of mitochondrial loss (C149). This is an important control that strengthens the overall model.

results.result: The calsyntenin-CaMKII-MAPK pathway protects against degeneration by acting before axon breakage and specifically prevents the transition from axon beading to breakage. Loss of calsyntenin or activation of CaMKII does not suppress degeneration after axotomy, and protected axons stop at the beading stage without progressing to breakage.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C153 define the stage at which the pathway acts through axotomy experiments and longitudinal imaging. The lack of protection after axotomy (C150) and the arrest at the beading stage (C152) support the conclusion that the pathway prevents the beading-to-breakage transition (C153). This is important for understanding the mechanism and suggests the pathway acts on early degenerative events rather than late clearance processes. The evidence is clear and well-interpreted.

results.result: The acidic domain of calsyntenin is not essential for its pro-degeneration function. CASY-1C with all acidic residues mutated to neutral residues restores strong degeneration, though to a lesser extent than wildtype.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 test the importance of the acidic region through mutagenesis. The partial restoration of function (C122) supports the conclusion that the acidic domain is not essential (C123), though the reduced effectiveness suggests it may have some role. The interpretation that the reduction may be due to secondary effects is reasonable but speculative. The conclusion is adequately supported for the claim made.
